title: How Sloths Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore sloths: their evolutionary history within the group Xenarthra (sloths, anteaters, armadillos), the two-toed (Choloepus) and three-toed (Bradypus) species and how they differ, their unusual anatomy (extra neck vertebrae, upside-down fur parting, multi-chambered stomach), extremely slow metabolism and movement, algae-covered fur and the sloth moth ecosystem, weekly defecation and its effect on the rainforest, defensive stillness, sleep, mating and maternal behavior (including a mother leaving a fallen baby), lifespan and difficulty keeping sloths in captivity, deforestation threats, and medicinal research on fungi from sloth fur. The episode opens with tour dates and a Kristen Bell sloth anecdote, and closes with a listener email about sharing political and religious opinions on the show.

segments.title: Live tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces upcoming SYSK Live tour dates in Chicago, Toronto, Boston, Portland, Florida, New Orleans and Brooklyn. The hosts banter about the guest producer, Kristen Bell's sloth birthday video, and sloths' bad fit for captivity.

segments.title: Sloth classification and evolution
segments.summary: The hosts describe sloths as members of the Xenarthra group with anteaters and armadillos, with origins in South America. They explain the two-toed and three-toed species, their differing toe and finger counts, and their distinct genera. A recent DNA study suggests they may have evolved independently.

segments.title: Sloth anatomy and the smiling face
segments.summary: The three-toed sloth looks like it is smiling because of fur coloring, not facial muscles. Sloths spend much of life upside down, which shapes their fur parting. The three-toed sloth has an extra neck vertebra, and sloths and manatees are the only mammals without seven neck vertebrae. Sloths also have a wide head-turning range.

segments.title: Sloth speed, name origin, diet and giant ground sloths
segments.summary: Sloths are very slow on the ground and in trees. The word sloth comes from Spanish 'perezosos' via English, and they are part of a seven deadly sins joke. Two-toed sloths are omnivorous, while three-toed sloths are picky leaf eaters. Giant ground sloths like megatherium walked on hind legs and were likely hunted by humans.

segments.title: Sloth metabolism, digestion and defecation
segments.summary: Sloth metabolism is far slower than human metabolism, producing under four watts. Digestion can take a month, and gas is reabsorbed and exhaled through the lungs. Sloths have a multi-chambered stomach and defecate about once a week at the base of trees.

segments.title: Sloth defense, sleep and algae-covered fur
segments.summary: Sloths stay still to camouflage from predators like harpy eagles. They sleep less in the wild than in captivity. Algae grows in grooves of their fur, giving them a green tint and a mini-ecosystem with beetles and sloth moths. The algae is fat-rich and may supplement their diet.

segments.title: Sloth poop, moths and rainforest nutrients
segments.summary: Sloth moths lay eggs in sloth feces, and the moths live only in sloth fur. Sloth droppings slow decomposition and fertilize the tree, benefiting the rainforest ecosystem. The hosts note this relationship between plant, animal and insect.

segments.title: Sloth mating, scent markers and babies
segments.summary: Sloths are solitary, and males and females mate very briefly. Males may leave scent markers on trees to attract mates, and females call with a high-pitched scream. Gestation lasts six to eleven months with a single baby. Mothers nurse briefly and carry young for six to eleven months. A mother may leave a fallen baby.

segments.title: Sloth lifespan, captivity and deforestation
segments.summary: Wild sloths live about twenty years, and captive ones often live longer. Predators are the main cause of sloth death. Sloths in captivity suffer stress and starvation because of their diet, and rehabilitation aims for release. Deforestation and roads threaten them, especially the pygmy sloth.

segments.title: Sloth fur fungi and medical research
segments.summary: Samples of fungi from three-toed sloth fur showed activity against malaria, Chagas disease, and human breast cancer cells, according to Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute research.

segments.title: Listener mail on political and religious opinions
segments.summary: A listener named Will says he values the hosts sharing opinions on religion and politics, as they challenge his views. The hosts thank him and invite other listener views. Sign-off and contact information are given.
